references.text: God calls Abram and gives him promises – an earlier example of God's revelation and intervention toward Abram.
God promises Abram a son and countless descendants, and Abram believes the Lord – background for the renewed covenant in chapter 17.
Abram was 86 years old when Ishmael was born. Thirteen more years passed until God revealed Himself to him again in 17:1.
God identifies Himself as 'El Shaddai' (אֵל שַׁדַּי) to Jacob, a direct parallel to God's self-presentation to Abram.
God says He revealed Himself to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as El Shaddai – confirming the name used in Genesis 17:1.
Noah walked with God (הִתְהַלֵּךְ) and was 'blameless' (תָּמִים) – a parallel to the command to walk before God's face and be perfect.
'You shall be blameless (תָּמִים) before the Lord your God' – a parallel to the command 'be perfect' in Genesis 17:1.
The book of Hebrews highlights Abraham's faith and obedience as examples, including his walk with God by faith.
Paul refers to Abraham's faith as the basis for justification, which is linked to God's covenant promises to Abraham.
Both verses show God's revelation to the patriarchs with the title El Shaddai, emphasizing God's almightiness and faithfulness in covenant history.
Both verses document theophanies where God reveals Himself to initiate new phases in Abraham's calling and covenant.
Both verses show God's revelation to Abram with a title that defines His relationship to him, combined with a call to trust and obedience.
The connection between God's demand for perfection (17:1) and Abraham's humble self-understanding (18:27) illuminates the tension in the holy life.
Genesis 17:1 describes the holy walk that is the natural fruit of the faith that justifies in Genesis 15:6.
Both verses use the title El Shaddai to confirm God's promise to make Abraham's offspring numerous, showing continuity in covenant history.
The connection between Abraham's call to walk before God's face (Gen 17:1) and the later longing to appear before God's face (Ps 42:3) illuminates the theme of God's presence.
